211.title: Cut down the forest (280–289)
211.hook: cut down the whole forest of desire, not just one tree; death sweeps off the distracted like a flood a sleeping village
211.howItsDone: Teachers in many Buddhist traditions quote the forest verse when explaining that practice aims at craving itself, not only at its separate outlets.

segments.voice: Yesterday, all created things: all made things pass, and nothing is a fixed self. Your line was all things pass. Today, the last day of chapter twenty, the way.

You decide to quit one thing. Say it's the late-night snack. You keep the promise for a week, and you feel strong. Then you notice you're scrolling until one in the morning instead. Or buying things you don't need. The snack was gone, but whatever wanted the snack just found another door. Anyone who has tried to change a habit knows this game of whack-a-mole. Today's verses name it with a picture that is also a pun.
screen: `QUIT ONE THING.` → `IT COMES BACK SOMEWHERE ELSE.` → `A PICTURE, AND A PUN.`

segments.voice: Verses two hundred eighty to two hundred eighty-nine close the chapter on the way. They open with a warning about the young and strong who never get around to rousing themselves: the path doesn't walk itself. Then verse two hundred eighty-three, in Max Müller's English: "Cut down the whole forest (of lust), not a tree only!" The bracket, of lust, is Müller's own, added to show what the forest stands for. Here's the pun. In Pali, vana means a forest, and vana also means desire, longing. So the Buddha is saying: cut down the vana, the forest and the wanting both. Chop down the snack tree, and the forest simply grows another one next to it. When you've cleared both the forest and the undergrowth, the verse goes on, you are free of the woods. The next verses show how deep the roots go. As long as desire is not cut, the mind stays tied, the text says, like a calf that won't leave its mother's side. Then comes the sharpest picture in the chapter. A man, proud of his children and his herds, with his mind on everything else, is carried off by death the way a flood carries off a sleeping village. In the night, while everyone dreams. One way to read it: desire keeps us from noticing time. Sons and fathers and relatives can't shelter anyone from it, the text goes on, and so the wise person, seeing this, clears the road now. Cutting one tree is still worth doing. But the aim is to look past the tree to the forest, the wanting underneath, and to start while the village is still awake.
screen: `ROUSE YOURSELF: THE PATH WON'T WALK ITSELF.` · `VANA — FOREST, AND DESIRE.` · `THE FLOOD AND THE SLEEPING VILLAGE.` · `CLEAR THE ROAD NOW.` · then, large: `CUT THE FOREST.`

segments.voice: Think of one small desire that came up today, a snack, a purchase, a check of the phone: just one tree. Gently look behind it for the wanting underneath, boredom maybe, or tiredness, or wanting to feel a little better, and name it quietly without fighting it. Then let the naming go and come back to the breath, in and out.
Vana. Pali for forest, and also desire: cut the whole wanting, not one tree.
Your line: cut the forest. The whole wood, not one tree. On to the next chapter.

a vow to give up one bad habit for good
an axe used for clearing the woods

212.title: The bigger joy (290–295)
212.hook: if by leaving a small pleasure one finds a great one, the wise leave the small
212.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use verse 290 to explain renunciation not as loss but as trading a lesser happiness for a greater one; the riddle verses 294–295 are usually taught with the commentary's symbolic reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vana: forest and desire both, so cut the whole wanting, not one tree. Your line was cut the forest. Today, chapter twenty-one begins.

There's a famous experiment with children and marshmallows: one now, or two if you can wait. The same trade turns up at the dinner table, when the phone buzzes while the person across from you is mid-story. Or the extra hour in bed, when the quiet morning walk was the plan. The small pleasure isn't evil. It just sits right in front of the bigger one, blocking the view. A chapter the translator simply called miscellaneous opens with exactly this trade.
screen: `ONE MARSHMALLOW NOW, OR TWO?` → `THE SMALL PLEASURE BLOCKS THE VIEW.` → `A CHAPTER CALLED MISCELLANEOUS.`

segments.voice: Chapter twenty-one gathers verses that didn't fit elsewhere, and it starts with a plain one. Verse two hundred ninety, in Max Müller's English: "If by leaving a small pleasure one sees a great pleasure, let a wise man leave the small pleasure, and look to the great." Notice the verse doesn't say pleasure is bad. The Pali word is sukha: happiness, ease, sweetness. The verse wants more of it, not less. It's a trade, and the wise person makes the good one. The next verse shows a bad trade: the one who seeks happiness for himself by causing pain to others gets tangled up in hatred and never gets free. Then the verses turn to attention. People neglect what ought to be done and do what ought not, the text says, and their desires keep growing; but those who keep watch over the body, moment by moment, don't drift that way. Then comes a startling pair, verses two hundred ninety-four and two hundred ninety-five. They say the true brahmana goes free, even after killing mother and father and two kings. Read on its own, it's shocking. The old commentary explains it as a riddle. The mother is craving, the father is pride, the kings are two wrong views, and the kingdom is the senses and everything that rides on them. Kill those, and you walk free. It's yesterday's forest, told as a riddle. The bigger joy, in the end, is the freedom on the far side of all the small trades.
screen: `SUKHA — HAPPINESS, EASE, SWEETNESS.` · `A BAD TRADE: JOY BUILT ON PAIN.` · `KEEP WATCH OVER THE BODY.` · `THE RIDDLE OF MOTHER, FATHER, KINGS.` · then, large: `THE BIGGER JOY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small pleasure you reach for most days, a second coffee, one more episode, a few more minutes in bed, and ask what bigger joy it sometimes stands in front of: a conversation, a rested morning, a clear head. You don't have to give anything up; just see the two side by side, the small and the great. Then let both go, and rest in the breath, which asks nothing of you.
Sukha. Happiness, ease: leave a small sukha when it hides a great one; the verse wants more happiness, not less.
Your line: look to the great. Small joy and great joy are both sukha. Day two hundred twelve.

guess: happiness, ease, a kind of sweetness
a selfish pleasure the wise must give up
the suffering that comes from wanting

213.title: Well awake (296–305)
213.hook: the disciples of Gotama are always well awake, day and night their minds on the Buddha, the dhamma, the sangha
213.carry: a mind that keeps returning home
213.howItsDone: Many Buddhists recall the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha at the start and end of the day, often with a bow and a short Pali homage before a home shrine; Theravada teachers call this recollection of the three jewels.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sukha: leave a small happiness when it hides a great one. Your line was look to the great.

What's the last thing on your mind before you fall asleep? For a lot of people it's the glow of a screen, a worry about tomorrow, or a replay of something awkward said at lunch. And the first thing in the morning is often the same worry, picking up where it left off. Whatever the mind rests on at the edges of the day tends to color everything in between. Today's verses describe people whose minds rest somewhere else, day and night, and they use the word that gives the Buddha his name.
screen: `THE LAST THING BEFORE SLEEP.` → `THE FIRST THING IN THE MORNING.` → `WHERE THE MIND RESTS.`

segments.voice: Verse two hundred ninety-six, in Max Müller's English: "The disciples of Gotama (Buddha) are always well awake, and their thoughts day and night are always set on Buddha." Gotama is the Buddha's family name. The words for well awake come from the same root as the word Buddha itself, budh, to wake up. A buddha is one who has woken, and his students, the verse says, are well awake too. Then the verse repeats like a chant, six times over. Well awake, their thoughts set on the Buddha. Then on the dhamma, the teaching. Then on the sangha, the community. Müller, writing in 1881, translated sangha as the church, which tells you something about his own world. Those first three are the three jewels from camp three, the three things Buddhists go to for refuge. The next three verses keep going: their thoughts set on the body, then delighting in harmlessness, then delighting in meditation. So well awake doesn't mean never sleeping. It means the mind has a home to return to. The rest of the chapter gathers other sayings. Leaving the world is hard, the text says, and living in a household is hard too; both have their pains. Good people shine from far away like the Himalayas, while the bad go unseen, like arrows shot at night. And the chapter ends with the one who sits alone, sleeps alone, walks alone, and finds joy in it, as if living in a forest. In many Buddhist homes, the three jewels are recalled at the end of the day, before sleep: a short homage, a bow, a moment of remembering.
screen: `BUDH — TO WAKE UP.` · `BUDDHA, DHAMMA, SANGHA, DAY AND NIGHT.` · `A HOME FOR THE MIND.` · `SHINING LIKE THE HIMALAYAS.` · then, large: `WELL AWAKE.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle as if it were bedtime, and let three things pass slowly through your mind, one with each breath: the Buddha, someone who woke up; the dhamma, the teaching and the way things are; the sangha, all the people, past and present, who have walked this path. If you're simply learning, just hold the three names, the way you'd hold three stones in your hand. Then rest with the breath.
Well awake. From budh, to wake, the same root as Buddha: a mind that keeps returning home, day and night.
Your line: a mind that keeps returning home. Buddha, dhamma, sangha, day and night. Rest well.

guess: a mind that keeps turning to the three jewels
a monk who has reached full awakening
someone who never needs to sleep at night

214.title: Grasp it rightly (306–311)
214.hook: the liar goes downward; kusa grass grasped wrongly cuts the hand
214.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the kusa-grass verse to warn that practice held with pride or harshness does harm; kusa grass itself was long used in India for mats and ritual, and the tradition says the Buddha sat on a bundle of it on the night of his awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, well awake: a mind that returns, day and night, to the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha. Your line was a mind that keeps returning home. Today, chapter twenty-two: the downward course.
screen: `WELL AWAKE — A MIND THAT KEEPS RETURNING HOME.`

segments.voice: Pull a blade of tall grass through your fingers the wrong way, and it can slice you like paper. The grass didn't change. The way you held it did. Pick it up by the base and pull it straight, and it comes away clean. Grab it along the edge, and it bites. In India there's a grass called kusa, sharp-edged, long used in ritual and for sitting mats. Today's verses use it to say something about how we hold even good things.
screen: `A BLADE OF GRASS CAN CUT.` → `KUSA — SHARP-EDGED, SACRED.` → `HOW YOU HOLD IT.`

segments.voice: Chapter twenty-two is called the downward course, and it speaks bluntly about what happens after harm. It opens with lying. The one who says what didn't happen goes downward, the text says, and so does the one who did something and says, I didn't do it. The downward course means rebirth in painful states, which Müller translates as hell; in Buddhist teaching these states don't last forever: they end when the karma that caused them runs out. The next verses aim at monks who wear the yellow robe but live badly. Better to swallow a red-hot iron ball, one verse says, than to eat the village's offered food while living that way. Then verse three hundred eleven, in Max Müller's English: "As a grass-blade, if badly grasped, cuts the arm, badly-practised asceticism leads to hell." Here's the surprise. The warning isn't about bad things. It's about good ones, held wrongly. The monk's life, the practice, the discipline, can cut you if you grab it by the edge. Held with pride, it becomes a way to feel superior. Held with harshness, it becomes self-punishment. Held with show, it becomes a costume. For anyone learning a path, including this one, it's a useful mirror. A daily sit, a precept, a kind act can each be held rightly, lightly and honestly, by the base. Or they can be held by the edge. The grass is the same either way.
screen: `THE DOWNWARD COURSE BEGINS WITH A LIE.` · `THE ROBE WITHOUT THE LIFE.` · `GOOD THINGS, GRASPED BADLY, CUT.` · `HOLD IT BY THE BASE.` · then, large: `GRASP IT RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open on your lap and think of one good thing you do regularly: a habit, a practice, a way you help someone. Ask gently how you're holding it, by the base, lightly and honestly, or by the edge, with a little pride or a little harshness toward yourself; no verdict needed, just notice the grip. Then let your hands stay open, and let the breath come and go on its own.
Kusa. A sharp-edged grass used for ritual mats: held by the edge it cuts the hand, so even a good practice, held badly, can hurt.
Your line: grasp it right. Even the good things need a careful grip. Day two hundred fourteen, done.

a soft reed woven into monks' robes
a thorny bush that marks a sacred grove

215.title: The frontier fort (312–319)
215.hook: guard yourself like a border town, guarded within and without
215.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics and lay practitioners train in guarding the sense doors, noticing what comes in through the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind; teachers often use the frontier-fort verse to describe it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kusa: sharp grass that cuts the hand when it's held by the edge. Your line was grasp it right. Today, the second day of the downward course.

A capital city has big armies and thick walls. A town on the frontier has neither. It sits at the edge, where trouble arrives first, and its people can't afford to be casual. They know which gate is weak, which stretch of wall is crumbling, which night the guards get sleepy. They check them all, every day, and inside the walls they keep order too. Today's verse takes a town like that as a picture of a person.
screen: `A TOWN AT THE EDGE.` → `TROUBLE ARRIVES FIRST.` → `THE WEAK GATE, THE SLEEPY GUARD.`

segments.voice: The downward course keeps going with plain advice. A slack effort, a vow half kept, a doubtful discipline: none of these brings much fruit. If something is worth doing, do it with your whole strength. A bad deed is better left undone, one verse says, because it burns you afterward; a good deed is better done, because it doesn't. Then verse three hundred fifteen, in Max Müller's English: "Like a well-guarded frontier fort, with defences within and without, so let a man guard himself." Within and without. The walls face outward, against what comes in through the senses: the ad, the insult, the easy temptation. But the fort also keeps watch inside, over the moods and thoughts that start their own trouble. Let no moment slip past, the verse goes on: those who let the right moment pass suffer for it later, in the downward course. The chapter's last verses are a surprise. They're about shame and fear aimed at the wrong target. Some people are ashamed of what isn't shameful, and not of what is. Some fear what isn't dangerous, and shrug at what is. They see wrong where there is none, and miss it where it is. So guarding the fort isn't being anxious about everything. A good guard knows which gate is actually weak. Buddhist teaching calls this guarding indriya-saṃvara, restraint of the senses: keeping watch at the doors of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind. It isn't a wall to hide behind. It's attention, placed where it's needed.
screen: `DO IT WITH YOUR WHOLE STRENGTH.` · `A FORT GUARDED WITHIN AND WITHOUT.` · `SHAME AND FEAR AT THE WRONG TARGET.` · `KNOW WHICH GATE IS WEAK.` · then, large: `GUARD THE BORDER TOWN.`

segments.voice: Walk the walls of your own town and ask where trouble usually gets in: a gate on the outside, like a certain app, a certain conversation, a certain time of night, or a gate on the inside, like a mood that turns sour or a thought that loops. Pick just one weak spot. Picture a calm guard standing there, not angry, just awake, and rest in the breath.
The frontier fort. A border town guarded within and without: watch the gates of the senses, and the mind inside.
Your line: guard the border town. Within and without, with a calm guard at the gate. See you tomorrow.

a wall you build to shut the world out for good
a soldier's lonely post at the edge of a kingdom

216.title: Bearing the arrow (320–324)
216.hook: as the elephant in battle bears the arrow, I will bear harsh words
216.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers pair verse 320 with the commentary's story of Magandiya's hired insults; khanti, patience, is trained as a daily practice and counted among the perfections in both Theravada and Mahayana teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the frontier fort: guard yourself within and without, and know which gate is weak. Today, chapter twenty-three, the elephant.
screen: `THE FRONTIER FORT — GUARD THE BORDER TOWN.`

segments.voice: Someone says something harsh about you. Online, across a table, or behind your back, and it comes around. Your body reacts before you do: face hot, heart fast, a reply already typing itself in your head. And a small voice says: let's just leave. Change the group chat, the job, the town. The old commentary on today's verse tells of a morning when the Buddha's companion said almost exactly that.
screen: `SOMEONE SAYS SOMETHING HARSH.` → `THE REPLY TYPES ITSELF.` → `LET'S JUST LEAVE.`

segments.voice: Verse three hundred twenty, in Max Müller's English: "Silently shall I endure abuse as the elephant in battle endures the arrow sent from the bow: for the world is ill-natured." The commentary's story: in the city of Kosambi, a woman named Magandiya held a grudge against the Buddha. She paid people to follow him and his monks through the streets, shouting insults. Ananda, a monk traveling with the Buddha, had had enough. Let's go to another town, he said. The Buddha asked: and if they abuse us there? Then another town, said Ananda. The Buddha said a problem should be settled where it arises, and he spoke this verse. The abuse, the story says, faded within a week. The picture is a war elephant, trained to walk into battle and take the arrows that come at it. A tamed elephant, the next verses say, is the one the king rides, and the best among people is the one who has tamed himself and can bear hard words. Mules, fine horses and great elephants are good when trained, but the one who trains himself is better still. No animal, however fine, can carry you to the untrodden place; only a tamed self goes there. Bearing isn't pretending it didn't hurt. The arrow still lands. The elephant just doesn't stampede. Buddhist teaching calls this khanti, patience or forbearance, one of the qualities a person on the path trains, again and again, one arrow at a time.
screen: `MAGANDIYA'S HIRED INSULTS.` · `ANANDA: LET'S LEAVE TOWN.` · `THE WAR ELEPHANT DOESN'T STAMPEDE.` · `KHANTI — PATIENCE THAT BEARS.` · then, large: `BEAR THE ARROW.`

segments.voice: Feet on the ground, heavy like an elephant, bring back one small criticism you've received lately, and notice where the words land in the body: the chest, the jaw, the belly. Don't argue with them, and don't agree either; just stand, feeling the sting without turning to trample, and breathe into that spot. Then let the criticism go, and rest with the breath.
Nāga. An elephant: like a war elephant that takes the arrow and doesn't stampede, this is patience with harsh words.
Your line: bear the arrow. Like the elephant, stand your ground. That's day two hundred sixteen.

a war horse trained to charge at the first arrow

217.title: Alone in the forest (325–333)
217.hook: if you find no good companion, walk alone like an elephant in the forest
217.howItsDone: Buddhist tradition values both good spiritual friendship and time in solitude; monks go on solitary retreats, and the Parileyya elephant who served the Buddha appears in Buddhist temple art.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nāga, the war elephant that takes the arrow and doesn't stampede: patience with harsh words. Today, the end of the week and of the elephant chapter.

A table for one. A weekend with no plans. A quiet apartment on a Saturday night. For some people, being alone can feel like proof that something's wrong, so it's tempting to fill the silence with company, even company that leaves you worse off. Today's verses have a different picture: a great elephant walking by itself through the forest, unhurried, needing nothing from the herd. The commentary says the Buddha himself once spent a rainy season like that, in a forest, with an elephant for a companion.
screen: `A TABLE FOR ONE.` → `COMPANY THAT LEAVES YOU WORSE.` → `AN ELEPHANT, UNHURRIED.`

segments.voice: The elephant chapter ends with verses about the mind and about company. First the mind: it used to wander wherever it pleased, one verse says, but now I will hold it, the way a trainer with a hook holds an elephant in rut. Pull yourself out of the bad road like an elephant pulling itself out of the mud. Then company. If you find a wise, good friend to walk with, walk with them gladly. If you don't, walk alone. Verse three hundred thirty, in Max Müller's English: "It is better to live alone, there is no companionship with a fool; let a man walk alone, let him commit no sin, with few wishes, like an elephant in the forest." The commentary sets these verses after a bitter quarrel among the monks of Kosambi, yesterday's city. The monks wouldn't make peace, so the Buddha left and spent a rains retreat in the Parileyya forest, where, the story says, a great elephant who had also left his noisy herd looked after him. Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say people are bad or that friendship is a trap. Earlier chapters praised good company, and the next verse says friends are sweet when need comes. Good company first; if that's missing, your own company, kept clean and simple, beats bad company. This week you cut the forest, traded for the bigger joy, stayed well awake, grasped it rightly, guarded the border town and bore the arrow. The elephant closes the week walking by itself, content.
screen: `HOLD THE WANDERING MIND.` · `A GOOD FRIEND FIRST.` · `IF NOT, WALK ALONE.` · `THE ELEPHANT OF PARILEYYA.` · then, large: `ALONE, NOT LONELY.`

segments.voice: For this sit, you are the elephant in the forest: no one needs anything from you, and you need nothing from anyone. Listen to whatever sounds are near, the way an elephant listens to the trees, and notice how it feels, a little strange, maybe, or a relief. If loneliness shows up, let it sit beside you like another animal in the clearing; you don't have to send it away.
Ekacara. One who walks alone: with no good companion, walk alone, with few wishes, like an elephant in the forest.
Your line: alone, not lonely. Your own company can be good company. Day two hundred seventeen, and a week, done.

original.note: Pali ekacara: one who walks alone; verse 330 uses the verb 'eko care' (let one walk alone).

trapdoor: what you thought: 'alone in the forest' means cutting yourself off from people.
what it means: good company first; if there's none, your own company, simple and clean, beats bad company.
what a scholar hears: the same image, 'eko care', echoes the Rhinoceros Sutta of the Sutta Nipata (Sn 1.3), and the Parileyya story is told in the Vinaya and the commentaries.
